lessons.title: F and J, the index fingers
lessons.tip: Welcome! Rest your index fingers on F (left hand) and J (right hand). These are your two guide keys, each with a small bump. Do not look at your keyboard: trust your muscle memory.

tuto.intro: Welcome to your very first lesson! Take 30 seconds to learn the basics of touch typing with ten fingers. It will change everything from here on.

rules.d: Rest your eight fingers on the middle row: A S D F for the left hand, J K L ; for the right hand. Your index fingers go on F and J, where you can feel a small bump. It is how you find your place without ever looking down.

rules.t: Keep your eyes on the screen
rules.d: Do not look at your fingers. Learning to stop looking at the keyboard is how you build the muscle memory that makes you truly fast.
Use your thumb for the long bar at the bottom, either one, whichever you prefer. A quick tap between groups of letters is all it takes.
Type slowly and accurately: every mistake builds a bad habit. Speed will come by itself once the movement is memorised.

tuto.tip: Goal: anchor your two index fingers by typing only F and J. Do not force it. Aim for steadiness, not speed.

lessons.text: fj jf fj jf fjfj jfjf ffjj jjff fjf jfj ffj jjf fjfj jfjf fj jf fj jf ffjj jjff

lessons.title: D and K, the middle fingers
lessons.tip: Your middle fingers rest naturally on D and K, right next to your index fingers. Keep your index fingers on F and J as anchors: every finger returns to its home key after each keystroke.

tuto.intro: Now add your middle fingers. D and K sit right next to your index fingers, on the same home row.

rules.d: Your left middle finger covers D and your right middle finger covers K. They rest naturally on these keys, right beside F and J.
Do not move your index fingers: they stay on F and J while your middle fingers type. This is what lets you find your way back without looking.
A light press is enough. Do not lift your whole hand: just let the finger drop down, then come back up to its place.

tuto.tip: Goal: type F D K J from memory, keeping all four fingers close to their home positions.

lessons.text: dk kd dk kd dkdk kdkd ddkk kkdd fd jk dj kf fdk jkd dfk kjd fdkj jkdf dkfj kjfd dk kd

lessons.title: S and L, the ring fingers
lessons.tip: Your ring fingers cover S and L. That is six fingers in place now. Think of a gentle arch: your fingers rest slightly curved, ready to strike without lifting your wrist.

tuto.intro: Place your ring fingers on S (left) and L (right). You now have six fingers resting on the home row.

rules.d: Ring fingers are less agile than your index and middle fingers, and that is normal. Go slowly: accuracy comes before speed.
Keep your fingers slightly curved, as if resting on a small ball. Your wrist stays relaxed and does not sink onto the desk.
After every S or L, the ring finger goes back to its place. Your index fingers on F and J remain your guides.

tuto.tip: Goal: type S and L without twisting your hand, returning to the home row every time.

lessons.text: sl ls sl ls slsl lsls ssll llss sd lk sf lj sdf lkj fsl jls sdfl lkjf slfd lsjk fdsl kjls sl ls

lessons.title: A and semicolon, the little fingers
lessons.tip: Your little fingers are the weakest, and that is normal. A on the left, semicolon on the right. Do not turn your whole wrist: just let the little finger stretch a little.

tuto.intro: Now for the little fingers: A on the left, semicolon on the right. They are the trickiest to tame. With them, your home row is complete: A S D F, then J K L ;.

rules.d: Your little fingers lack strength and precision at first. Everyone starts here, even the pros. Be patient.

rules.t: Do not drag the whole hand
rules.d: Only stretch the little finger towards A or ;. If you swivel your wrist, your other fingers lose their place.
The little finger tends to stay in the air. Bring it back to its home key as soon as it has struck.

tuto.tip: Goal: bring your little fingers into action without breaking your home position. Go slowly and stay steady.

lessons.text: a lad asks dad; dad adds salad; all lads fall; sad lads ask; alas; a flask falls; dad adds a salad

lessons.title: G and H, the inner index fingers
lessons.tip: G and H are typed by your index fingers stretching slightly towards the centre. Keep the movement small: the finger slides, it does not jump. Return to F or J after each keystroke.

tuto.intro: G and H are in the middle of the keyboard. Your index fingers stretch a little to reach them.

rules.d: Your left index finger slides right for G, and your right index finger slides left for H. It is a small sideways movement, not a jump.
Straight after G or H, bring your index finger back to its home key. These are the home-row keys furthest from your starting position.

rules.t: Do not mix up the hands
rules.d: G is always typed with the left index finger, and H always with the right. Keep this rule firmly in mind.

tuto.tip: Goal: cover the whole middle of the home row without moving your other fingers.

lessons.text: gh hg; dad had half a salad; all glad lads shall ask dad; flags flash; a glass falls; ah; gas; hash; sag; lag

lessons.title: Review: the whole home row
lessons.keys: a s d f g h j k l ;
lessons.tip: A full review of the home row. This is your base: all your fingers return here after every keystroke. Take your time: steadiness matters more than speed.

tuto.intro: You now know the whole home row, the row your fingers always come back to between keystrokes.

rules.d: All your fingers start from this row and return to it. Mastering it means knowing where you are on the keyboard without looking.
This exercise mixes all ten keys. If you hesitate, slow down: the aim is to find them from memory, not to type fast.
Between keystrokes, feel that your eight fingers have gone back to A S D F and J K L ;.

tuto.tip: Goal: pass the whole home row with your fingers anchored and your eyes on the screen.

lessons.text: asdf jkl; glad lads ask dad; dad has half a salad; a flag falls; all dads shall ask

lessons.title: R and U, index fingers reaching up
lessons.tip: R is typed by the left index finger and U by the right. Your index fingers leave their home keys, move up one row, then drop straight back. Keep your other fingers resting on the home row.

tuto.intro: You move on to the top row, the one just above your home row. We start with the index fingers: R for the left hand, U for the right.

rules.t: The index finger goes up, then back down
rules.d: Your left index finger goes up to R, just above F. Your right index finger goes up to U, just above J. After each keystroke, it returns to its bump.
While one index finger reaches up, your other seven fingers stay on the home row. This is how you find your keys again without looking.
With R and U you can already write us, far, full, dark, hard and sugar. Read the whole word before you type it.

tuto.tip: Goal: reach up to R and U with your index fingers, then return to F and J without looking.

lessons.text: ru ur; us all; full glass; dark grass; a dark hall; full flask; dad has sugar; hard sugar falls; full hall; us

lessons.title: E and I, the middle fingers on the top row
lessons.tip: E is typed by the left middle finger and I by the right, just above D and K. Your middle finger goes straight up and drops back to its home key.

tuto.intro: E and I are typed with the middle fingers, above D and K. They are two very common letters in English: you will meet them all the time.

rules.t: The middle finger goes straight up
rules.d: Your left middle finger goes up to E, just above D. Your right middle finger goes up to I, just above K. It drops straight back to its home key.
Your index fingers stay on F and J while your middle fingers work: they are your guides for getting back without looking.
With E and I, words multiply: she, here, red, hair, desk, file, high. Type them slowly, letter by letter.

tuto.tip: Goal: type E and I without lifting your other fingers, and return to D and K each time.

lessons.text: ei ie; she is here; he has red hair; her ear is red; she read a file; he asked her; his desk is high

lessons.title: W and O, the ring fingers on the top row
lessons.tip: W is typed by the left ring finger and O by the right, above S and L. Ring fingers are less agile: go slowly and keep your wrist steady.

tuto.intro: W and O are typed with the ring fingers, above S and L. Both are very common in English: we, was, would, look, good, work.

rules.d: Your left ring finger goes up to W, above S. Your right ring finger goes up to O, above L. A small, precise movement is enough.

rules.t: Go gently with the ring fingers
rules.d: These fingers are less agile than your index and middle fingers. Aim for steadiness: a slow, accurate movement beats a fast, wrong one.

rules.t: A letter that comes up often
rules.d: You will find W in we, was, were, where, would, work and walk. Type them slowly, keeping your wrist steady.

tuto.tip: Goal: type W and O cleanly with your ring fingers, without twisting your hand.

lessons.text: wo ow; we were glad; she was slow; he would look for a good house; we work here; where is his dog; we walk

lessons.title: Q and P, the little fingers on the top row
lessons.tip: Q is typed by the left little finger and P by the right, right at the ends of the row. Keep your wrist steady and let only the little finger stretch.

tuto.intro: Q and P are typed with the little fingers, at either end of the top row. These are your weakest fingers, so give them time.

rules.d: Your left little finger goes up to Q, above A. Your right little finger goes up to P, above the semicolon. It is a demanding movement: go slowly.
Do not lift your whole hand to help the little finger. Your wrist stays steady and only the little finger stretches.

rules.t: Q is almost always followed by U
rules.d: In English too, Q is almost always followed by U: queue, square, equal. Learn them as a single movement. As Q is rare, the lesson also drills it with a short run of letters.

tuto.tip: Goal: master Q and P without breaking your position, even if your little finger still lacks strength.

lessons.text: qp pq; pupils queue up; square paper; a square; queue; square; queue; push a ship; help

lessons.title: T and Y, the inner index fingers on the top row
lessons.tip: T is typed by the left index finger and Y by the right: your index fingers stretch towards the centre to reach them. Return to F and J straight after the keystroke.

tuto.intro: T and Y are in the middle of the top row. Your index fingers stretch inwards to reach them: T for the left hand, Y for the right.

rules.d: Your left index finger goes up and slides right for T. Your right index finger goes up and slides left for Y. Keep the movement small.
Straight after T or Y, bring your index finger back to its home key. These keys are a little far away: do not lose your position.
With T you can write the, that, they, story, type, and even a short sentence: they stay at the shop.

tuto.tip: Goal: reach T and Y with your index fingers without moving your other fingers, then return to F and J.

lessons.text: ty yt; they stay at the shop; that is a story; the pupil is happy today; she sits here; they play late

lessons.title: Review: the whole top row
lessons.keys: q w e r t y u i o p
lessons.tip: You now master two full rows. During this review, focus on moving smoothly between rows: going from home to top should happen without lifting your wrists off the desk.

tuto.intro: You now know two whole rows. This review mixes all the letters of the top row.

rules.d: The challenge is no longer each key, but the move between rows. Going from the home row to the top row should feel smooth.
Do not lift your wrists to change rows: only your fingers move up and down.
Try to read two or three words ahead. Your brain prepares your fingers while you type.

tuto.tip: Goal: move between the home row and the top row without looking, with a smooth finger movement.

lessons.text: qwer tyui op; the girl is quite happy today; she wrote a letter; the pupils queue; he is quite tired

lessons.title: V and M, the index fingers on the bottom row
lessons.tip: V is typed by the left index finger and M by the right: your index fingers go down one row, below F and J, then return to their bump. Keep your other fingers resting on the home row.

tuto.intro: You move down to the bottom row, the one just below your home row. We start with the index fingers: V for the left hand, M for the right.

rules.t: The index finger goes down, then back up
rules.d: Your left index finger goes down to V, just below F. Your right index finger goes down to M, just below J. After each keystroke, it returns to its bump.
To reach down, curl your finger instead of stretching your whole hand. Your wrist may drop very slightly, but stays relaxed.
With V and M you can write me, mum, milk, very, have and visit. And a sentence: we have a very warm home.

tuto.tip: Goal: reach down to V and M with your index fingers, then return to F and J without looking.

lessons.text: vm mv; mum has milk; we have a very warm home; they visit a valley; we have five; move over

lessons.title: C and comma, the middle fingers on the bottom row
lessons.tip: C is typed by the left middle finger and the comma by the right, below D and K. The comma sticks to the word before it, then a space follows.

tuto.intro: C and the comma are typed with the middle fingers, below D and K. The comma is your first punctuation mark: it makes sentences easier to read.

rules.d: Your left middle finger goes down to C, below D. Your right middle finger goes down to the comma, below K. The movement goes down, not sideways.

rules.t: The comma sticks to the word
rules.d: Type the word, then the comma straight away with no space before it, then a space after: cake, cheese, coffee. Tidy punctuation makes your texts easy to read.
Your index fingers stay on F and J while your middle fingers reach down: they are your guides for getting back without looking.

tuto.tip: Goal: reach down to C and the comma without losing the home row, with a relaxed wrist.

lessons.text: c, ,c; cake, cheese, coffee, rice; cold cloud; coat, scarf, sock, cat; the teacher, the class, the school

lessons.title: X and full stop, the ring fingers on the bottom row
lessons.tip: X is typed by the left ring finger and the full stop by the right, below S and L. The full stop ends the sentence: it sticks to the last word.

tuto.intro: X and the full stop are typed with the ring fingers, below S and L. X is fairly rare but useful. The full stop ends every one of your sentences.

rules.d: Your left ring finger goes down diagonally to X, below S. Your right ring finger goes down to the full stop, below L. Do it slowly to learn it.

rules.t: The full stop ends the sentence
rules.d: It sticks to the last word, then a space follows: the taxi is here. the fox is there. For now, we write without capital letters.

rules.t: Go gently with the ring fingers
rules.d: These fingers are less agile than your index and middle fingers. A slow, accurate movement is better than a fast, wrong one.

tuto.tip: Goal: place X and the full stop with your ring fingers, without lifting your whole hand.

lessons.text: x. .x; six foxes. six taxis. the taxi is here. the fox is there. six.

lessons.title: Z and forward slash, the little fingers on the bottom row
lessons.tip: Z is typed by the left little finger and the forward slash by the right, at both ends of the bottom row. Let only the little finger stretch, and keep your wrist steady.

tuto.intro: Z and the forward slash are typed with the little fingers, at the ends of the bottom row. These are your weakest fingers, so give them time.

rules.d: Your left little finger goes down to Z, below A. Your right little finger goes down to the forward slash, far right, after the full stop. Do not turn your whole hand.
You see it in his/her, mum/dad, he/she. It is typed with no space on either side.
You will find it in zero, zoo, lazy, size, prize and pizza. Practise it with words and with short runs of letters.

tuto.tip: Goal: master Z and the forward slash with your little fingers, without breaking your position.

lessons.text: z/ /z z/ /z; pizza, zero, lazy, zoo; his/her; mum/dad; he/she; prize; size; puzzle

lessons.title: B and N, the inner index fingers on the bottom row
lessons.tip: B is typed by the left index finger and N by the right: your index fingers stretch towards the centre to reach them. Return to F and J straight after the keystroke.

tuto.intro: B and N complete the alphabet. Your index fingers stretch towards the centre, right at the bottom: B for the left hand, N for the right. With them, you have all 26 letters.

rules.d: Your left index finger goes down and slides right for B. Your right index finger goes down and slides left for N. Keep the movement small.
Straight after B or N, bring your index finger back to its home key. These are the keys furthest from your starting position.
With B and N, you know the whole alphabet. From here on, you can write whole sentences, even though you do not have capital letters yet.

tuto.tip: Goal: reach B and N with your index fingers without moving your other fingers, and enjoy having finished the alphabet.

lessons.text: bn nb; the new bike is blue. a brown bear is on the beach. nine big birds, ten nice bags.

lessons.title: Review: all 26 letters together
lessons.keys: z x c v b n m , . /
lessons.tip: Every letter is here. The aim of this review: no glances at the keyboard. If you hesitate over a key, pause, find it in your mind, then type.

tuto.intro: You now know the whole bottom row, so every letter of the alphabet. This review mixes all three rows.

rules.t: Do not look at the keyboard
rules.d: If you hesitate over a key, pause, find it in your mind with your finger, then type. Do not look down.
Top, middle and bottom rows become a single movement: each finger goes up, goes down and returns to its home key.
The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog: this classic sentence contains all 26 letters. If you can type it without looking, you know your keyboard.

tuto.tip: Goal: move through all three rows without looking, with a smooth finger movement.

lessons.text: zxcv bnm,./ the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.

lessons.title: Rhythm and two-syllable words
lessons.tip: You have every letter now. Type these two-syllable words at a regular pace, like a metronome: steadiness matters more than speed.

tuto.intro: You have every letter now. Time for rhythm: chain together two-syllable words to make your typing flow.

rules.d: Type the syllables at an even pace, like a metronome. Steadiness is better than fast, jerky bursts.
Your brain does not type letter by letter but in small groups. Feel each syllable (ba-by, lem-on, riv-er) as a single movement.
Keep your shoulders and wrists loose: tension breaks your rhythm and tires your hands.

tuto.tip: Goal: find a steady, flowing rhythm on two-syllable words.

lessons.text: baby lemon river finger table funny garden window village coffee ticket pencil

lessons.title: Essential function words
lessons.tip: Small words (the, and, but, for, with...) turn up in every sentence. Typing them in one go makes you faster everywhere.

tuto.intro: Small function words (the, and, but, for, with...) turn up in every sentence. Making them automatic helps you everywhere.

rules.d: These words make up a huge share of any English text. The more automatic they are, the faster you type overall.
Aim to type each small word in a single go, without thinking letter by letter.
Read the next word while your fingers finish the one before.

tuto.tip: Goal: type function words without hesitation, as reflexes.

lessons.text: the and but for with this that they from have will would you can not are she her his him who how

lessons.title: Common everyday words
lessons.tip: A word repeated often enough ends up typing itself. Keep your rhythm all the way along the line, even on a longer word.

tuto.intro: We widen the range to common everyday words. The bigger your stock of automatic words, the smoother your typing becomes.

rules.d: A word repeated often enough ends up typing itself. That is the goal: it frees your mind to think about the meaning.
Do not slow down suddenly on a longer word. Keep an even pace across the whole line.
If a word trips you up often, slow down on it for a few repetitions, then pick the tempo up again.

tuto.tip: Goal: chain common words together with ease and regularity.

lessons.text: house table chair door book pencil desk bag bus bike car phone window kitchen garden school bread milk rice apple coffee

lessons.title: Everyday vocabulary
lessons.tip: Longer words: break them into small movements, keep your typing clean rather than rushed, and let your eyes catch the end of the word while you type the start.

tuto.intro: Verbs and longer words. A chance to hold your rhythm on words with several syllables.

rules.d: A long word is typed as a string of small movements: lis-ten, car-ry, vis-it. Think in chunks.
The longer the word, the more a mistake costs you. Keep your typing clean rather than rushed.

rules.t: Look ahead to the end of the word
rules.d: While you type the start, your eyes have already caught the end. Let your fingers follow.

tuto.tip: Goal: type longer words without breaking your rhythm or accuracy.

lessons.text: walk talk read write listen learn teach carry climb jump swim play work visit open close drink move start stop leave

lessons.title: First natural sentences
lessons.tip: You move on to real sentences. The challenge is no longer the key, but the flow from start to finish: type in groups of words, with the comma and full stop tucked tight against the words.

tuto.intro: You move on to real sentences. The challenge is no longer the key, but how smoothly you get from one end of the sentence to the other.

rules.d: Read and type in small groups (the children / walk / to school) rather than one isolated word at a time.
The space is hit with your thumb, without breaking your rhythm. It is the most used key on the keyboard.
The comma and full stop stick to the word before, then a space follows. Capital letters come later: for now, we write in lowercase.

tuto.tip: Goal: type whole sentences in one continuous, flowing movement.

lessons.text: the children walk to school. the teacher opens the door, and we read a book. it is a good day.

lessons.title: Left-hand capitals (right Shift)
lessons.keys: Q W E R T A S D F G
lessons.tip: For a left-hand letter, hold the right Shift key with your right little finger. Hold Shift, type the letter, release.

tuto.intro: To write a capital letter, you hold down the Shift key, then type the letter. The golden rule: use the Shift key on the opposite hand to the letter. We start with the left-hand letters.

rules.d: Hold Shift with the little finger of the hand that is NOT typing the letter: right Shift for a left-hand letter, left Shift for a right-hand letter. Both hands work together.
Press Shift and keep it down, type the letter, then let go of both. If you release Shift too early, you will get a lowercase letter.

rules.t: Words in capitals, and words with Q
rules.d: Here, several words are written entirely in capitals (WATER, GREAT): you hold Shift for the whole word. Words that start with Q (Queen, Quick) have just one capital, at the start.

tuto.tip: Goal: type left-hand capitals with the right Shift key, without hesitating.

lessons.text: Queen Quick Quiet Queue Quite Quake Quarter Question WATER GREAT STREET SWEET DESERT GRASS STARS WEST WEAR WASTE WET WE WAS EAST FAST FAT FED FAR FEW DAD DEAF DRAW FEAR GATE GAS GET GRADE STAGE DEGREE FREE

lessons.title: Right-hand capitals (left Shift)
lessons.keys: Y U I O P H J K L
lessons.tip: For a right-hand letter, hold the left Shift key with your left little finger. The same movement as before, on the other side.

tuto.intro: Same principle, on the other side: for a right-hand letter, you hold the left Shift key with your left little finger.

rules.d: Hold Shift with the little finger of the hand that is NOT typing the letter: right Shift for a left-hand letter, left Shift for a right-hand letter. Both hands work together.
Press Shift and keep it down, type the letter, then let go of both. If you release Shift too early, you will get a lowercase letter.
Phil, Jill, Kylie, Kyle, Lily, Judy: names start with a capital letter. Words in capitals (HILL, POOL, YOU) make you hold Shift for longer.

tuto.tip: Goal: type right-hand capitals with the left Shift key, and alternate with the left hand.

lessons.text: Phil Jill Jack John Kylie Kyle Lily Judy Hope Jane JOLLY YOU JOY JOY HILL KILO YOLK POOL LOOK PUPIL YOU YOU HIP HIP HOP HOLY HI OIL PULL UP KILO JOKE JUMP LUCK HOUR KIND

lessons.title: Bottom-row capitals
lessons.keys: Z X C V B N M
lessons.tip: For Z X C V B, hold right Shift. For N M, hold left Shift. The same rule: the hand opposite the letter.

tuto.intro: The bottom-row capitals are left. The rule does not change: Shift on the opposite hand. Z, X, C, V, B for the left hand; N and M for the right hand.

rules.d: Hold Shift with the little finger of the hand that is NOT typing the letter: right Shift for a left-hand letter, left Shift for a right-hand letter. Both hands work together.
Press Shift and keep it down, type the letter, then let go of both. If you release Shift too early, you will get a lowercase letter.
With these seven letters, you know all 26 capitals. From here on, you can write proper names and the start of sentences.

tuto.tip: Goal: type the bottom-row capitals on both sides, choosing the right Shift key.

lessons.text: Zero Zoo Max Victor Nick Manchester Mark Molly ZOO ZERO ZOOM ZEBRA BOX MIX SIX FIX TAXI EXTRA VAN CAVE COVE COSY ZIP NOW MUM NINE CLUB BUS CAB VIVID EXAM CIVIC NOVEL CUB BAN SIX BOX NEXT NONE ZOO ZIP

lessons.title: Proper names and cities
lessons.tip: The names of people, cities and countries start with a capital letter. Keep your rhythm: Shift, letter, then the lowercase letters in one smooth run.

tuto.intro: Proper names, those of people, cities and countries, start with a capital letter. A chance to mix everything you have just learned.

rules.d: Oxford, York, Paris, Emma, Harry, Oscar: for each proper name, one Shift movement, then the lowercase letters in a flow.
Do not slow down after the capital: Shift and the letter form a single movement, and the lowercase letters follow.
Spot the next proper name before you reach it: your hand already knows which Shift key it will need.

tuto.tip: Goal: chain proper names together without breaking your rhythm.

lessons.text: Oxford, York, Derby, Paris, Liverpool, Manchester, Wales. Emma, Harry, Holly, Henry, Jane, Oscar, Lucy, Mark, Peter.

lessons.title: Correctly capitalised sentences
lessons.tip: A sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop. After the full stop, a space, then the capital letter of the next sentence.

tuto.intro: A sentence always starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop. You put it all into practice in real sentences.

rules.d: After the full stop, type a space, then the capital letter that opens the next sentence. This is a movement to make automatic.
Emma, Harry, Paris, Oxford: in the middle of a sentence, a proper name keeps its capital letter.
Before typing a word, ask yourself: start of a sentence? Proper name? If so, use the opposite Shift.

tuto.tip: Goal: type whole sentences with their capital letters, without hesitating over the Shift key.

lessons.text: Emma and Harry go to Oxford. They take a train with Oscar. It will be a good day in Oxford.

lessons.title: The colon: Shift + semicolon
lessons.tip: The colon is on the same key as the semicolon: hold Shift with your left little finger and press the key with your right little finger.

tuto.intro: The colon introduces a list or an explanation. On QWERTY, it shares the semicolon key: you get it with Shift. The exact movement for your keyboard is shown just below.

rules.d: Hold Shift with your left little finger (the opposite hand), press the semicolon key with your right little finger, then release.
In English, you never put a space before : ; ? or !. It goes word, sign, space. The sign sticks to the word before it.
Here is my list: bread, milk, rice. The colon announces what follows: a list, an explanation, a quotation.

tuto.tip: Goal: type the colon with Shift + semicolon, tucked tight against the word before it.

lessons.text: Here is my list: bread, milk, rice. Three words: calm, kind, quiet. Note: it is late. Look: the sun is out. Remember: stay calm. Two things: tea, milk.

lessons.title: The apostrophe
lessons.tip: The apostrophe is the key to the right of the semicolon, typed with your right little finger. On a US International keyboard, it is a dead key: press it, then the space bar.

tuto.intro: The apostrophe marks a contraction (don't, it's, she's) or possession. It is very common in English. The exact movement for your keyboard is shown just below.

rules.t: To the right of the semicolon
rules.d: It is typed with your right little finger, on the key just right of the semicolon, without Shift.
On US International, the apostrophe is a dead key: press it, then the space bar, otherwise it combines with the next letter to make an accented letter. On a plain US keyboard, it works straight away.
Type the start, the apostrophe, the end, with no space at all: don't, it's, can't, she's, they're.

tuto.tip: Goal: type the apostrophe with the right movement for your keyboard, with no space around it.

lessons.text: It's late and she's tired. We don't know. She can't come, but she's glad. That's fine. They're here.

lessons.title: The hyphen
lessons.tip: The hyphen is the key to the right of the 0, at the top right: your right little finger reaches up to it, without Shift. It joins compound words.

tuto.intro: The hyphen joins compound words (part-time, well-known, check-in, mother-in-law). The exact movement for your keyboard is shown just below.

rules.d: Your right little finger reaches up to the key to the right of the 0, without Shift. That is the hyphen key.
No space around the hyphen: mother-in-law, part-time, well-known, check-in.

rules.t: Do not confuse it with the underscore
rules.d: The underscore (_) on the same key needs Shift: it comes later, with the symbols. Here, it is the plain hyphen.

tuto.tip: Goal: reach up to the hyphen with your right little finger and return to the home row.

lessons.text: Her mother-in-law has a part-time job in a well-known shop near the check-in desk. We eat ice cream. She has a T-shirt.

lessons.title: The question mark: Shift + forward slash
lessons.tip: The question mark is on the same key as the forward slash: hold Shift with your left little finger and press the key with your right little finger.

tuto.intro: The question mark ends a question. On QWERTY, it shares the forward slash key: you get it with Shift. The exact movement for your keyboard is shown just below.

rules.d: Hold Shift with your left little finger, press the forward slash key with your right little finger, then release.
In English, you never put a space before : ; ? or !. It goes word, sign, space. The sign sticks to the word before it.
Where is the dog? What is your name? A single question mark at the end of the question is enough.

tuto.tip: Goal: type ? with Shift + forward slash, tucked tight against the last word.

lessons.text: Where is the dog? What is your name? How old are you? Do you like tea? Is it cold? Can you help? Who is there?

lessons.title: The exclamation mark: Shift + 1
lessons.tip: The exclamation mark is on the 1 key, at the top left: hold Shift with your right little finger and press 1 with your left little finger.

tuto.intro: The exclamation mark sets the tone: emotion, an order, surprise. On QWERTY, it is on the 1 key: you get it with Shift. The exact movement for your keyboard is shown just below.

rules.d: Hold Shift with your right little finger (the opposite hand), press the 1 key with your left little finger, then release.
In English, you never put a space before : ; ? or !. It goes word, sign, space. The sign sticks to the word before it.
Stop! Well done! One exclamation mark is enough: avoid piling them up.

tuto.tip: Goal: type ! with Shift + 1, tucked tight against the last word.

lessons.text: Stop! Look out! Well done! What a day! Happy birthday! Welcome home! Good luck! Thank you! Hello!

lessons.title: Brackets and quotation marks
lessons.tip: Round brackets are on the 9 and 0 keys, and straight quotation marks are on the apostrophe key: all need Shift, held with your left little finger.

tuto.intro: Round brackets set aside an extra detail, and quotation marks surround speech. On QWERTY, all three need Shift, with keys on the right hand. The exact movement for your keyboard is shown just below.

rules.d: Hold Shift with your left little finger. The opening bracket is on 9, the closing bracket on 0, and the quotation mark on the apostrophe key.
Every bracket or quotation mark you open must be closed. Practise chaining the opening, the text, then the closing without hesitating.
They surround speech: He says: "hello". English uses these straight quotation marks on the keyboard.

tuto.tip: Goal: type ( ) and " with Shift, opening then closing.

lessons.text: Tom (ten) says: "hello". Anna (nine) says: "thanks" (again). Dad (at work) says: "wait" (please). Mum (at home) says: "yes".

lessons.title: Punctuation in real text
lessons.tip: You bring all the punctuation together in a real text. Spot the next mark in advance, and get ready with Shift if needed.

tuto.intro: You bring all the punctuation together in a lively text: hyphens, apostrophes, quotation marks, brackets, exclamation and question marks.

rules.t: Spot the mark that is coming
rules.d: Before you reach a mark, know which one it is: direct (apostrophe, hyphen, comma, full stop) or with Shift (? ! : ( ) ").
Each mark that needs Shift uses the Shift key opposite the mark's own key: it is the same rule as for capital letters.
Correct punctuation makes a text easy to read and professional. Take your time: speed will come.

tuto.tip: Goal: chain all the punctuation together in a text, without breaking your rhythm.

lessons.text: "Come quickly!" he says. She replies: "Wait for me; it's late." It is a well-known story (really). Who is there? Mum!

lessons.title: 4 5 6 7: the index fingers reaching up
lessons.tip: Your index fingers cover four numbers: the left one 4 and 5, the right one 6 and 7. They reach up two rows, type, then drop back to F and J.

tuto.intro: The number row is right at the top of the keyboard, above the top row. We start with the index fingers, which cover the most numbers: 4 and 5 for the left hand, 6 and 7 for the right.

rules.t: The index finger reaches up two rows
rules.d: Your left index finger goes up to 4 and 5, your right to 6 and 7. The movement starts from F and J, crosses the top row and comes back.
On a QWERTY keyboard the number row is direct: one press is enough, with no Shift. The symbols that share these keys (! ? ( ) and so on) are the ones that need Shift.
After each number, your finger drops back to its home key. Your other fingers do not move: this is what lets you never look down.

tuto.tip: Goal: type 4 5 6 7 with your index fingers, then return to F and J without looking.

lessons.title: 3 and 8: the middle fingers
lessons.tip: Your left middle finger reaches up to 3, your right middle finger to 8. Keep your index fingers anchored on F and J.

tuto.intro: Now the middle fingers: 3 for the left hand, 8 for the right. They go straight up, above E and I.

rules.t: The middle finger goes straight up
rules.d: Your left middle finger goes up to 3, above E. Your right middle finger goes up to 8, above I. A straight movement, without pivoting your hand.
Your index fingers stay on F and J while your middle fingers reach up: they are your guides for getting back without looking.
On a QWERTY keyboard the number row is direct: one press is enough, with no Shift. The symbols that share these keys (! ? ( ) and so on) are the ones that need Shift.

tuto.tip: Goal: type 3 and 8 with your middle fingers, keeping your other fingers resting.

lessons.title: 2 and 9: the ring fingers
lessons.tip: Your left ring finger reaches up to 2, your right ring finger to 9. These fingers are less agile: go slowly.

tuto.intro: The ring fingers cover 2 and 9. We are nearing the edges of the row: these fingers are less agile, so we go slowly.

rules.d: Your left ring finger goes up to 2, above W. Your right ring finger goes up to 9, above O. The movement is longer: stay precise.
The further you get from the centre, the more mistakes creep in. Slow and accurate beats fast and wrong.
On a QWERTY keyboard the number row is direct: one press is enough, with no Shift. The symbols that share these keys (! ? ( ) and so on) are the ones that need Shift.

tuto.tip: Goal: reach 2 and 9 with your ring fingers, without looking.

lessons.title: 1 and 0: the little fingers
lessons.tip: Your left little finger reaches up to 1, your right little finger to 0, at both ends of the row. Let only the little finger stretch.

tuto.intro: The little fingers cover 1 and 0, at both ends of the number row. These are your weakest fingers, so give them time.

rules.d: Your left little finger goes up to 1, above Q. Your right little finger goes up to 0, above P. Do not turn your whole hand.
Your wrist stays steady and only the little finger stretches. Do not lift your whole hand to reach 1 or 0.
On a QWERTY keyboard the number row is direct: one press is enough, with no Shift. The symbols that share these keys (! ? ( ) and so on) are the ones that need Shift.

tuto.tip: Goal: type 1 and 0 with your little fingers, without breaking your home position.

lessons.title: Review: all the numbers
lessons.tip: You know the whole number row. Chain the numbers in every direction: the aim is to find them without looking.

tuto.intro: You now know all ten numbers. This review mixes them every which way to fix each movement.

rules.d: Rising runs, falling runs, alternating runs: each number must come without hesitation, whatever the sequence.
A date or a room number is typed in small groups of two or three digits. Feel each group as a single movement.
After each number, your finger drops back to its home key. Your other fingers do not move: this is what lets you never look down.

tuto.tip: Goal: chain all ten numbers without looking at the keyboard.

lessons.title: Numbers in real text
lessons.tip: Numbers mix with letters: times, addresses, phone numbers. Keep your rhythm as you move between the letter rows and the number row.

tuto.intro: In real life, numbers mix with letters: times, headcounts, room numbers. That is what you type here.

rules.d: Moving from one row to another must stay smooth: reach up to the number, type it, then drop back to the home row.
42, 8.30, 105: spot the group of digits before you reach it and type it in one go.
One mistake in a number changes everything. Slow down on the numbers if needed: speed will come with repetition.

tuto.tip: Goal: type numbers in the middle of a text without losing your rhythm.

lessons.text: There are 42 pupils in 3 classes of 14. Bus 12 leaves at 8.30. Room 105.

lessons.title: $ % ^ &: the index fingers
lessons.tip: These four symbols are on the 4, 5, 6 and 7 keys with Shift: your index fingers reach them, just as for the numbers.

tuto.intro: The symbols on the number row are typed with Shift. We start with those of the index fingers: $ and % on 4 and 5 for the left hand, ^ and & on 6 and 7 for the right hand. The exact movement for your keyboard is shown just below.

rules.d: Just like capital letters: hold Shift with the little finger of the hand that is not typing the key. Shift plus the number key gives the symbol.

rules.t: The same keys as the numbers
rules.d: You already know these keys: 4 5 6 7. Only the Shift press changes. Your index finger reaches up, types, and drops back to F or J.
On a US International keyboard, ^ ~ and ` are dead keys: type the symbol, then press the space bar so that it appears on its own.

tuto.tip: Goal: type $ % ^ & with Shift and the index fingers, without looking.

lessons.text: $name $total $price $cost $one $two 50% 25% 10% 75% 5% 90% 3^2 2^4 5^3 7^2 2^3 6^2 R&D fish&chips salt&pepper tea&milk bread&butter mum&dad

lessons.title: # and *: the middle fingers
lessons.tip: The hash is on the 3 key and the asterisk on the 8 key, with Shift: your middle fingers reach up.

tuto.intro: The middle fingers cover the hash # (3 key, left hand) and the asterisk * (8 key, right hand). The hash starts a hashtag, and the asterisk is used in sums and lists. The exact movement for your keyboard is shown just below.

rules.d: Just like capital letters: hold Shift with the little finger of the hand that is not typing the key. Shift plus the number key gives the symbol.
#news #help #music: a word preceded by # is a hashtag. Type the hash, then the word, with no space.
3*4 reads as "three times four". You also see it as a marker or a wildcard.

tuto.tip: Goal: type # and * with Shift and the middle fingers.

lessons.text: #news #help #sport #travel #food #music 3*4 5*6 7*8 2*9 *note* *tip* *hello* #ok

lessons.title: @: the at sign
lessons.tip: The at sign is on the 2 key, with Shift: your left ring finger reaches up, with right Shift.

tuto.intro: The at sign links a person's name and the domain of an email address: anna@mail.example. On QWERTY, it is on the 2 key, with Shift. The exact movement for your keyboard is shown just below.

rules.d: Just like capital letters: hold Shift with the little finger of the hand that is not typing the key. Shift plus the number key gives the symbol.

rules.t: The heart of an email address
rules.d: info@shop.example: the name, @, then the domain. No spaces are allowed in an address.
The ring finger is less agile than the index finger: reach up gently to the 2, and hold Shift with your right little finger.

tuto.tip: Goal: type @ with Shift + 2, in complete addresses.

lessons.text: hello@school.example anna@mail.example jack@work.example info@shop.example @emma @tom @lucy mark@home.example

lessons.title: _ + =: the right little finger
lessons.tip: The underscore, plus and equals signs are on the keys to the right of the 0: your right little finger reaches right to the end of the row.

tuto.intro: Right at the end of the number row, your right little finger reaches three signs: the underscore _ (Shift + hyphen), the plus + (Shift + equals) and the equals = (no Shift). The exact movement for your keyboard is shown just below.

rules.d: The keys to the right of the 0 are the furthest away: stretch only your little finger, and keep your wrist steady.
_ and + need Shift (with your left little finger); = is typed on its own. The plain hyphen seen earlier is the _ key without Shift.
my_name, file_name, a+b=c: the underscore joins words in code names, and the plus and equals signs do sums.

tuto.tip: Goal: reach _ + = with your right little finger, returning to the home row.

lessons.text: a+b=c x_y my_name file_name 2+3=5 total_score a_b+c_d 4+4=8 one_two 1+1=2 9=9 big_cat+dog=pets

lessons.title: ` and ~: the left little finger
lessons.tip: The backtick and the tilde are on the key at the top left, under Esc: your left little finger reaches it, with Shift for the tilde.

tuto.intro: Right at the top left, your left little finger reaches the key for the backtick ` and the tilde ~ (with Shift). You see them in code and in file paths: ~/documents. The exact movement for your keyboard is shown just below.

rules.t: The left little finger reaches up
rules.d: This key is to the left of the 1. Your left little finger reaches it; the tilde needs Shift with your right little finger.
On a US International keyboard, ^ ~ and ` are dead keys: type the symbol, then press the space bar so that it appears on its own.
`code` wraps a piece of code; ~/documents points to the home folder. Two signs, one single stretching movement.

tuto.tip: Goal: type ` and ~ with your left little finger, using the right movement for your keyboard.

lessons.text: `code` ~/documents `npm install` ~user `name` ~/music `tab` ~/home `end` ~/desktop ~/photos

lessons.title: Review: the number-row symbols
lessons.tip: You bring all the number-row symbols together in a text. Identify the finger and the Shift key before you go for the sign.

tuto.intro: You bring the number-row symbols together in a text: addresses, prices, sums, variable names, paths. The exact movement for your keyboard is shown just below.

rules.t: Identify the sign before typing it
rules.d: Which finger? Which hand for Shift? This reflex saves you time on every symbol.
The movement is always the same: opposite-hand Shift, the key, then release both.
A wrong symbol breaks an address or a command. Slow down on the ones that give you trouble.

tuto.tip: Goal: chain all the number-row symbols together in real text.

lessons.text: hello@school.example $name 50% a&b #tag 3*4 x_y 2+3=5 `code` ~/home 3^2 info@shop.example 10% a+b=c

lessons.title: [ ]: square brackets
lessons.tip: Square brackets are to the right of P, at the very end of the top row: your right little finger reaches up to them, without Shift.

tuto.intro: Square brackets [ ] are typed with your right little finger, on the two keys to the right of P. They are used in code (list[0]) and for added words in square brackets. The exact movement for your keyboard is shown just below.

rules.d: Your right little finger stretches past P: [ is just to the right, ] just after it. No Shift is needed.
Every bracket you open must be closed. Chain it together: open, type, close.
list[0], data[3], item[i]: the square bracket picks out a slot in a list.

tuto.tip: Goal: type [ and ] with your right little finger without leaving your home position.

lessons.text: list[0] list[1] [a] [b] item[i] names[2] [yes] [no] [end] data[3] [1] [2]

lessons.title: { }: curly braces
lessons.tip: Curly braces are on the same keys as square brackets, with Shift: your right little finger reaches up, and your left little finger holds Shift.

tuto.intro: Curly braces { } share the keys of the square brackets: you get them with Shift. You meet them in code and stylesheets. The exact movement for your keyboard is shown just below.

rules.d: Just like capital letters: hold Shift with the little finger of the hand that is not typing the key. Shift plus the number key gives the symbol.
Like square brackets: a brace you open must be closed. Get into the habit of typing them in pairs.
{style: bold}, {x: 1}: braces mark out a block of code or an object.

tuto.tip: Goal: type { and } with Shift and your right little finger.

lessons.text: {a} {b} {x: 1} {y: 2} {end} {ok} {style: bold} {name: tom} {yes} {no}

lessons.title: \ and |: backslash and vertical bar
lessons.tip: The backslash and the vertical bar are on the key just above Enter, typed with your right little finger; the vertical bar needs Shift.

tuto.intro: The backslash \ and the vertical bar | share one key, right at the end of the top row, above Enter. You get the vertical bar with Shift. The exact movement for your keyboard is shown just below.

rules.d: Your right little finger stretches to the end of the top row, past the square brackets. \ is typed on its own, | with Shift.
C:\Users\Tom: the backslash separates folders in Windows, whereas the plain forward slash / separates them elsewhere.
a | b joins two commands or separates two choices: left | right.

tuto.tip: Goal: type \ and | with your right little finger, with Shift for the vertical bar.

lessons.text: C:\Users\Tom a|b a||b c\d \n \t left | right /home | grep \\ || C:\Windows

lessons.title: < >: angle brackets
lessons.tip: Angle brackets are on the comma and full stop keys, with Shift: your right middle and ring fingers reach down, and your left little finger holds Shift.

tuto.intro:
Angle brackets < > are typed with Shift on the comma and full stop keys. You see them in HTML tags:

text

. The exact movement for your keyboard is shown just below.

rules.d: Just like capital letters: hold Shift with the little finger of the hand that is not typing the key. Shift plus the number key gives the symbol.

text

: the opening bracket, the name of the tag, the closing bracket. The forward slash / closes the tag.
Every tag you open is closed with the forward slash. Practise chaining the two.

tuto.tip: Goal: type < and > with Shift and the fingers of your right hand.

lessons.text:

lessons.title: Review: all the symbols in text
lessons.tip: We bring all the symbols together in a text mixing an address, the web, code and prices. Spot the movement before each symbol: direct, Shift or dead key.

tuto.intro: We bring all the symbols together in a text mixing an email address, the web, code and percentages. The big mix! The exact movement for your keyboard is shown just below.

rules.d: Shift, dead keys, direct signs: each symbol has its own movement. Use everything you learned in the last two modules.
Before each symbol, identify it: direct, Shift or dead key? This reflex saves you time.
Mastering the symbols means typing an address, a piece of code or a formula without ever getting stuck.

tuto.tip: Goal: chain all the symbols together in real text, each movement at the right moment.

lessons.text: hello@school.example (twelve) https://shop.example #tag {css: bold} <html> 50%=ok a+b=c [end] ~/home "value" 3*4 C:\Users a|b

lessons.title: Linking short sentences
lessons.tip: Do not stop between sentences: the full stop, the space and the capital letter flow in the same movement.

tuto.intro: Time for speed. We chain short sentences together to work on flow from start to finish.

rules.d: Do not stop between sentences. The full stop, the space and the capital letter flow in the same movement.
Keep your eyes a step ahead of your fingers: it is the secret of fast, smooth typing.
Speed comes from suppleness, not force. Relax your shoulders and wrists.

tuto.tip: Goal: chain short sentences together with no dead time between them.

lessons.text: The sun comes up. The birds sing. The tea is ready. We go out together. Come on, quickly! Have a good day.

lessons.title: Natural medium-length sentences
lessons.tip: On a long sentence, do not freeze if you make a mistake: keep going. Type in groups of words that go together.

tuto.intro: Longer sentences, as in real life. The aim: hold your rhythm over time.

rules.d: On a long sentence, do not freeze if you make a mistake: keep going. Keeping the flow matters most.
Type in groups of words that go together, not word by word. The sentence becomes a string of small bursts.
The longer the sentence, the more a mistake costs. Aim for a speed you can hold cleanly.

tuto.tip: Goal: type a medium-length sentence in a single flow, without losing your rhythm.

lessons.text: Every morning, she opens the window and breathes the fresh air before she starts a busy day at work.

lessons.title: A full narrative paragraph
lessons.tip: A paragraph takes stamina: settle into a comfortable rhythm you can keep up to the end, without taking your eyes off the screen.

tuto.intro: A whole paragraph to type. This is about stamina: keeping your focus and steadiness to the end.

rules.d: A paragraph takes stamina. Settle into a comfortable rhythm that you can keep up without getting tired.

rules.t: Keep your eyes on the screen
rules.d: The longer the text, the stronger the temptation to look at the keyboard. Keep your eyes ahead.
Commas, full stops and apostrophes are part of the flow. Fit them in without breaking your pace.

tuto.tip: Goal: type a complete paragraph at a steady pace, from start to finish.

lessons.text: Typing without looking at your hands takes patience, but a little practice every day makes you faster and calmer. It is just a habit.

lessons.title: Professional text
lessons.tip: A professional text leaves no room for approximation: polite phrases, capital letters, careful punctuation, numbers and an address.

tuto.intro: A professional-style text: an email or letter, with an address and a number. The kind of text you will really write.

rules.d: Polite phrases, capital letters, careful punctuation: a professional text leaves no room for approximation.
Numbers, emails, @: you mix everything you have learned. It is the summary of your learning.
In a professional setting, accuracy matters as much as speed. Proofread in your head as you type.

tuto.tip: Goal: type a clean professional text, with letters, numbers and symbols mixed.

lessons.text: Dear Mrs Hall, please find our offer attached. Do not hesitate to contact us by email at info@shop.example. Kind regards, Peter Grey

lessons.title: Technical text with symbols
lessons.tip: Code and configuration: braces, quotation marks, paths and numbers. Spot the movement for each sign in advance.

tuto.intro: The full challenge: code and configuration, with braces, quotation marks, paths and numbers.

rules.d: Braces, quotation marks, colons, numbers... This text keeps Shift and the dead keys busy all the way through. It is the densest test in symbols.
Spot in advance whether the next sign is direct, needs Shift or needs a dead key. Preparation prevents getting stuck.
In code, one mistake breaks everything. Here, slow and exact beats fast and sloppy.

tuto.tip: Goal: type a technical text mixing code, symbols and numbers cleanly.

lessons.text: The file settings.json holds {"version": "1.0", "mode": "test", "port": 3000}. Run `npm start` in ~/project.

lessons.title: Speed sprint: a long text
lessons.tip: The final test: a long text to type as fast and as accurately as you can, without looking at the keyboard.

tuto.intro: The final test: a long text to type as fast and as accurately as you can. Give it everything!

rules.d: Now is the time to test your limits. Look for your top speed while staying readable.
A clean sprint beats a sprint full of mistakes. Find the point where you go fast without skidding.
If you type this text without looking at the keyboard, you have reached the goal of KeyPace. Congratulations!

tuto.tip: Goal: type a long text at your top speed, without looking at the keyboard.

lessons.text: Fast typing comes from regular practice: train a little every day, keep your eyes on the screen, and let your fingers find their place on the keyboard. Good luck!
